system.summary: Three layers used together inside one word. (1) About 25 letter signs, one per letter (c is a large double-barred sign, g a small single-bar one). (2) A syllable table in alphabetical order, 432-525: a row of five for the vowels (434 is a stop or null) and for each consonant b c f g h j k l m n p r s t v w z (ba 437 ... zu 525); the d row has four (447 de to 450 du; da is the word code 158). (3) Numbers 1-430: words, names and frequent syllables (78 ge, 117 be, 389 ver, 290 lich, 210 Schweden, 326 Churfürst). 106 of them have a value in map v4; well over a hundred seen in the letters have none. Clear text and cipher alternate within the sentence. Not the image-55 key (K55) of the Høeg and Meyercron letters in targets/biermann1675.
system.notes: distinct_symbols, nulls.count and nomenclator.unread_groups are not counted (0 is a placeholder): the number of distinct open codes over the 27 letters was not enumerated for this folder (an earlier tally over 12 letters gave 123). entries counts the word-code values of map v4. Letters can be written by a sign or inside a table syllable or a word-part code, hence homophones. key_order: the syllable table is alphabetical; no order has been found in 1-430.

prior_solution.where: None found; priority not established. Checked 11-12 Nov 2026: this repository (targets/biermann1675 lists the Klingenberg family as key unknown, not attempted; its key-volume sweep found no sheet that reads it, sheet 94/95 only in part); Dudout, L'Europe chiffrée (Klingenberg named only); web searches. Not checked: Rigsarkivet guide nos. 278 and 327 (Klingenberg's legation archive, journal and letterbook of 1675, where the received letters may stand deciphered); Klingenberg's embassy journals of 1665-67; NLA Oldenburg Best. 20-44 Nr. 8; Wegener, Aarsberetninger VI.

conditions.human_role: Malcolm McBratney directed the work, set the rules (every attempt recorded, transcriptions frozen before decoding, held-out letters, shuffled controls, no claim without its check) and sent the result; Claude sessions chose the letters from the repository's survey, transcribed, solved, read and checked. No reading by a person without AI.
tools: own Python: tokeniser, decoder, strict and lenient counter (scripts/count.py; the first versions in scripts/original/)
German quadgram model for the syllable-table fit
models: Claude (Anthropic), several sessions of 11-12 Nov 2026 (model ids not recorded)
claude-fable-5-2 (session of 12 Nov 2026 that prepared this folder)

solution.what: The repository's lead, Chiffer sheet 94/95, tested on the Klingenberg letters: held-out letters 0 of 305 and 0 of 144. Not the key.
Letter signs from a probable word, requisition, which also stands in the clear text of the 6 February letter, and from repeats.
Syllable table 437-525 as alphabetical rows, from alliierten and other repeated forms, fitted on four March letters; 16 March held out: 36 of 157 tokens strict with the table alone.
Greedy fit of the 30 most frequent numbers below 430 to German function words with a quadgram model: degenerate (er, in, ge everywhere).

Word-code values from two or more independent contexts in training letters: map v1 (29 May held out, 284 of 437), v2 (17 April held out, 165 of 239), v3 with 78 values (4 May held out: 551 of 729 = 75.6%). A parser fault of the first scripts (lines beginning with the sign # skipped) was found and fixed.

Word-map values shuffled over the same codes, 5,000 times, each letter re-scored against its gloss: 0 of 5,000 reach the real count on any letter. The gloss was written after decoding by the same judge, so this control is weaker than it looks.

Seven untouched copybook letters (8 May to 24 June), each transcribed, frozen and decoded once with v3 unchanged: 2,006 of 2,524 tokens (79.5%). Then map v4 (106 values). Three drafts from the next archive unit, decoded once with v4 unchanged: 1,091 of 1,456 (74.9%).

Check by Daniel Bourdeau on issue 424: a decoder written from the key reproduces all 452 sign and syllable tokens of the 4 May letter; 331 of 333 tokens agree with images 166-168; two numerals corrected (447 for 441, probably 501 for 511); 0 of 5,000 for shuffled keys with a German model on the signs and the table; the word-code layer only weakly separated by a character model; 54 open-code tokens, not 42.

For this folder: both numerals checked on the images (447 certain, 501 probable); every figure of the issue recomputed (counts.txt); rule-built readings with every hole in place; full English for the 4 May letter and the three drafts only.

outcome.method_basis: No key sheet and no decipherment: signs from a probable word and repeats, the syllable table from its alphabetical structure, word-code values from repeated contexts in the letters themselves, each map frozen before the letter it was tested on.
outcome.fraction_read_source: counts.txt (scripts/count.py): over the eleven letters that were each decoded once with a map frozen beforehand, 3,648 of 4,709 cipher tokens decode exactly to the judge's intended word (4 May 551 of 729; seven copybook letters 2,006 of 2,524; three drafts 1,091 of 1,456). Codes with no value in the map are never counted. The judge's glosses were written after decoding and have not been checked by a second reader.

gaps.item: Word codes with no value (54 tokens of the 4 May letter under v3; 25 under v4)
gaps.detail: Mostly names and nouns seen once to five times: 143, 418, 71, 353, 112, 180, 352, 329, 416, 385. More letters, or Klingenberg's own deciphered letterbook, would fix them.

gaps.item: The sign for c against the sign for g in the three drafts
gaps.detail: Our reader wrote every hash-like sign as # (c). 96 failed tokens sit in words that differ from the intended word only by c for g. A blind re-reading of those glyphs is not done; no figure that assumes it is quoted.

gaps.item: English translations of the eleven letters by a model
gaps.detail: Translations by Claude, not checked by a German-reading person. The punctuation and word division of the German readings are ours (the cipher marks neither); no decoded letter was changed.

gaps.item: Sixteen further letters (6 February to 21 June) used to build the key
gaps.detail: Transcriptions and decryptions in texts/; no reading and no count of record, since the key was built on them. 20 March is its first page only.

gaps.item: Glosses by one judge, written after decoding; transcriptions by one reader who knew the key
gaps.detail: A second gloss exists for 29 May only (304 of 329 spans agree). No blind second transcription of any letter.

gaps.item: Clear text between the cipher passages
gaps.detail: Read approximately; one long clear passage of the 4 May letter only in part.

gaps.item: Prior decipherment in Klingenberg's own papers
gaps.detail: Rigsarkivet guide nos. 278 and 327 not checked; priority is not established.

texts.label: Biermann to Klingenberg, 4 May 1675
texts.note: read_share is our count of the README word rule on the cipher passages of the reading file (232 words, 93 holes); the clear passages (lines beginning >) are not counted. By cipher tokens under the map of record the figure is in counts.txt.
texts.summary: The King has read with surprise that the allies hold him bound to break with Sweden while giving no subsidies for his fleet. The treaty point on the fleet is conditional, but Sweden must be hurt at sea, which cannot be done without a fleet, and Sweden will equip hers; war without a fleet would leave Sweden a free hand. The King has more men on foot than the treaties stipulate and agrees to a muster in his own lands. He has told the resident 'Brendt' how unwillingly he sees the Elector left without earnest support, and takes it as an example; if the allies' principals go on so, he and the Elector can part from the affair with advantage and reputation. Klingenberg is referred to the last letter about co-signing the declaration of war on Sweden. Context: the Scanian War; the Elector of Brandenburg was at The Hague in May 1675.

reading_review.by: Claude (Anthropic), for Malcolm McBratney: a model reading, not a person, and not independent (the session that prepared these files). Offered so the entry is complete; the reviewer's own record should replace it before merging.

texts.summary: Chancellor Brandt, the Elector of Brandenburg's envoy, has arrived in Copenhagen and handed in his commission in writing; Biermann expects him to get a written resolution soon, with all possible and [?reasonable] satisfaction. The King will not enter into rupture with Sweden before the allies have performed their side of the treaties, of which there is [21] likelihood or possibility. The Swedish ambassador extraordinary has handed in a new paper, which is to rest until the secretary sent to Sweden returns.

texts.summary: The King has read the reports on the allies' conclusion at The Hague, which Klingenberg and Høeg accepted; though it is not in accordance with his instructions and in many points contrary, he will not disavow them, and he awaits the particulars. They are to press for prompt payment of the remaining and fleet subsidies and the arrears of Anritzgelder, for ships manned for landings and put at the King's disposal, and to divert the allies' plan to send the Lüneburg troops to Flanders: they are needed on the Elbe, and without them the King will hardly proceed to the rupture. [413] [385] salt ships from Lisbon are said to be on the way, whose capture could open the war.

texts.summary: Klingenberg's report was laid before the Privy Council, and Biermann sends the list of regiments and companies of the stipulated [16] thousand men. The King agrees that the three thousand boatmen be taken on with his commissaries' billets and pay, as far as possible from his own subjects who are still free [?] (ledig). Høeg's mission to the Elector is not yet decided but will probably go ahead; 6,000 Swedish men are said to stand ready to cross to Germany.

texts.summary: Nothing is added on the Lüneburg troops beyond the dispatch of 25 May. The Swedish ambassador Count Niels Brahe has formally presented his king's marriage suit, and after long delay the King has declared through [193] that it is not contrary to him, with the express rider that the marriage shall not prejudice his treaties with the allies or their execution; Klingenberg is to remove any umbrage the States and the allies take. The King goes to Holstein next week to inspect his troops at Rendsburg and will propose a meeting to the Duke of Gottorp. Context (general knowledge, not from a source here): probably Charles XI of Sweden's suit for the Danish princess Ulrika Eleonora, 1675.

texts.summary: The King's departure for Holstein is put off to Monday, and the allied ministers, especially Brandenburg's, have been assured again that the Swedish marriage will not keep him from his obligations. Klingenberg's report of the 11th shows the remaining subsidies, Anritzgelder and fleet money unpaid (the province [327] has made a beginning), only [98] [...] of the stipulated warships at sea and the Lüneburg troops marching to the Netherlands, though the whole work rests on these points. Chancellor Brandt's paper argues that the sooner the allies are done with Sweden the sooner they will [189] to a [?reasonable] [34]; Høeg's dispatch for his journey to the Elector should be ready soon.

texts.summary: The King has read Klingenberg's report on the six points. Although the declaration of war will not be made in the name of all the allies at The Hague but by a [251] in his own territory, the points still unsettled must be negotiated according to the King's [377], above all payment of all outstanding moneys and of the [233] subsidies, since he has his troops together and needs the large subsidies for their keep. The Swedish ambassador takes his leave as the King leaves for Holstein, and Frantz Möller is to report fleet money to Guldensparre and land subsidies to von Stöcken by every post.

texts.summary: The King cannot see what the [377] given by the States General to their ambassador bound for [?Moscow], on peace between the [?Grand Duke] and the Turks, can serve but to unsettle the [244]; a peace might free the [258] to turn on the [100], so the [244] should rather be brought into action against Sweden by any means. The King declines to pay a share of the present for the [244]'s [?chancellor], having already spent heavily without repayment; the 16,000 stipulated men stand ready for muster, and Spain and the States are to pay the [233] subsidies from the month the troops were ready. The Swedish marriage will not keep him from his obligations; deputies from Gottorp have arrived.

texts.summary: Once 'this matter' is concluded the King will advance towards the borders and take measures for the common cause; when the nine warships reach the Sound, part of his fleet is to join them to harm Sweden. The States should ready more ships and send them after the first, for Sweden is busy putting a considerable fleet to sea.

texts.summary: Talks with the Elector's chancellor Brand in Copenhagen should soon conclude. The promised warships are awaited in the Sound so that no succour reaches Field Marshal Wrangel from Sweden. It is astonishing that the ships stay away while the allies press the King to make the rupture and blame him, though the ships are missing, a large part of the subsidies is in arrear and nothing of the large ones is paid: the States and Spain seem to hold the work up themselves. Klingenberg is to guard the King's interest at The Hague; the King would rather be given the further subsidy to strengthen his own troops.

texts.summary: The allies still think the King not in earnest; he has more cause to accuse them: the treaties require the conditions to be met before he proceeds to rupture, and neither subsidies nor Anritzgelder nor fleet money are fully paid, and only one of the stipulated ships has reached the Sound. Even so he has gathered the promised men, fitted out the fleet and brought [112] to hand over fortresses and troops, breaking the collusion with Sweden. The envoy in Moscow is to second the arriving Imperial ambassadors.
